tasks.title: A status row folds as the hook's echo only when the hook recorded that its call began before the verb row, so a later call's real restart keeps its charge
tasks.description:
`_echoes` in audit-task.py decides whether a repeated status row is the journal-writes hook's echo of the verb row before it. If it is an echo, the row folds and does not count as a restart. This is the third round on the same fail-open. Each earlier round inferred the echo from what the rows happen to share: first the session, then the session plus a 610 s window. An adversarial review (scratchpad/p142-44-adv/, the orchestrator gives the full path; repro_failopen.py) still folds a real restart. The sequence: a verb blocks the task, something outside any tool call moves it back, and a later Bash call in the same session blocks it again inside the window. That row folds, and `_ran_within` answers False.

Stop inferring. Redesign so the echo is proven from what the hook records:
1. journal-writes.py writes, on every status row it derives, the moment its own tool call began. That is the PreToolUse baseline time the row's `from` was read at. The PreToolUse sweep already keeps that baseline; carry its time.
2. `_echoes` folds a hook row only when it records that start, the start is at or before the verb row's stamp, and the hook row is in the same journal file as the verb row (the same tree). A row that lacks the field is a row written before this change. For those, keep today's bounded reading, named in the code as the reading for rows that carry no start, so the history does not change its answers. Re-run p142-44-adv/scan.py and report that no live answer changed.
3. Lows from the same review, in the same functions:
   - `_hook_run` ends a run when a same-file row from another writer is stamped between the edit row and its derived row (repro_run.py). Bind the derived row to its edit row by what the hook writes, not by adjacency. For example, the derived row carries the edit row's hash, or both carry one call id.
   - Branch 1 does not require the same tree (repro_tree.py).
   - The docstring and hw21's text claim "inside the tool call that wrote the verb's row", which a gap cannot show.
   - The 610 s derivation misses permission waits, MCP calls and BASH_MAX_TIMEOUT_MS. Once item 2 holds, state what the window still bounds, and only that.
Red-first a case for each repro. The hook stays importless and stdlib-only, and its import budget (tools/bench-hooks.py --gate) must hold. No F/P/BUG ids in comments.

tasks.title: A redo moves no tree: the old tree stays where it is under a kept marker and the new tree is cut at a fresh path, so no state between a move and git's agreement exists to classify
tasks.description:
A redo keeps the old task tree, so nothing a reading of it misses is lost. Today it keeps the tree by MOVING it: rename to `<tree>.aside-<n>`, lock git's record, repair, repoint submodules, and `repair_asides` settles an unfinished move at the start of every drive step. Four adversarial review rounds in a row each found a med in that machinery: a prunable record between rename and repair; classification by directory; a wedge on a gone record; a stop on a tree moved to a third path whose remedy orphans it. Probes are in scratchpad/p142-43-adv/, p142-43-adv/r2/ and p142-45-adv/ (the orchestrator gives the full path). The class is the move itself: every state between "renamed" and "git agrees" is one more case to classify.

Redesign so the redo moves nothing:
- The old tree stays where it is. Only its marker is rewritten to the keptTrees key, and that key is recorded, so task-add never adopts it and status lists it.
- The new tree is cut at a fresh path beside it. `add_tree` already passes `--path`.
- `wave.trees[task]` then names the new path, and the carry ref and everything else follow `wave.trees`.

That deletes the rename, the lock, the repair, the submodule repoint, `asideMoves`, `_settle_move`, `repair_asides` and its per-step call, the git 2.30 floor and the STATE_WRITERS row for the rename, together with their cases. Delete them; do not keep them dormant.

What stays:
- the one keep-on-doubt remover `remove_task_tree`, still read strictly;
- `retire_asides`;
- the per-tree status remedies, with the remedy for a kept old tree being one that acts on it. `git worktree remove` refuses a tree with a submodule checked out, so do not name that bare; name what works, and say what `--force` deletes.

Also:
- State where a second and third redo cut their trees, and that a path already taken is never reused.
- A crash between the marker rewrite and the state write must leave a state the next step reads correctly. The tree is at its own path, so only marker and state can disagree. Settle that by the marker, which is what task-add reads.
- Check every reader of `wave.trees` and `tree_path` that assumes the task's tree is at the default path: retire, close_wave, the sweep's kept-tree reason in _worktrees.py, and status. List each in your outcome.

Red-first a case that a redo leaves the old tree's directory and git record untouched (same path, same admin dir, not locked), and keep every case that proves no work is lost. No F/P/BUG ids in comments.

tasks.title: prove-gates runs its rows in parallel, each in an isolated worktree of the checkout, so the live tree is never mutated and a phase-wide probe fits the sign-off bound
tasks.description: MEASURED 2026-10-28: P142 sign-off stopped because meta.buildCommands.lintProbe (python3 tools/prove-gates.py --changed <70 phase paths>) ran 116 rows (67 red, 49 allow) serially and took about 74 min against drive-phase SIGNOFF_STEP_SECONDS=3600. A manual rerun was green on every row and left the tree unchanged, so the defect is the shape: rows run one at a time, each mutating the ONE live checkout via redfirst.sh, on a 10-core machine. Raising the bound is not the fix (the table only grows; the bound is tied to the gate's). DESIGN: prove() runs each row in a worker tree, never in the live checkout. Create a pool of worker trees (git worktree add --detach at HEAD, under a mkdtemp scratch outside every checkout) that mirror the checkout's current content (HEAD plus the tracked working-tree diff and untracked non-ignored files), so a by-hand run on a dirty tree still proves what the author is looking at. Run tools/redfirst.sh FROM the worker tree (it resolves its root from its own path) over a work queue across worker count = cores minus two (every core when CI=true, same rule as sweep-selftests.py). Each row keeps its own scratch TMPDIR as now. Results are collected and rendered in the table's order, so output stays byte-stable regardless of scheduling. Worker trees are removed in finally (git worktree remove --force plus prune) and a run that is killed leaves nothing registered that a later run cannot clean. The mutation marker (_suite.hold) protected the live tree from a concurrent sweep; decide from the code whether it is still needed once the live tree is never written, and state the answer in the comment. The drive's lint_probe compares the checkout around the run - it must now see no change by construction. Update the docs that say prove-gates mutates the tree and restores each time (CLAUDE.md Tests section, CONTRIBUTING.md, PLUGIN-BUILD-GUIDE.md) to say what is now true. New selftest cases (in prove-gates' own --selftest, which mutates nothing) for: ordering is stable, worker count rule, the worker tree mirrors a dirty tracked file and an untracked file, cleanup leaves no registered worktree. Measure a full --changed run with the P142 phase paths (git diff --name-only 0dfae3e7...HEAD minus docs/audit) before and after, and report both wall clocks.

openChoices: The selection's miss rate is read from two sources: a mutation replay over recent task commits and the real red runs in CI's history. Whether a miss in either blocks trusting the selection, or only a real one, is the owner's call; the recommendation is either
Tree scanners leave task gates: a task that breaks a whole-tree lint lands red on its phase branch until the phase gate catches it before merge
The sweep target of four minutes may need CPU to fall as well, because total CPU over the local worker count bounds the wall clock from below
The browser gates stay with the orchestrator and run serially; a task gate includes them only when the selection says the surface changed
